howToUpdate: Curated by mgmt-ops. Schema and rules: header of tools/lib/progress.mjs. Check: node tools/console.mjs progress --check. Plain words in title/fixes/felt/gate/next/why; jargon in details. Every phone number carries its tag (OBSERVED/CONFIRMED), driver and ref. No URLs, addresses or names.
goal: On the iPhone, scrolling with your finger should feel smooth: no frame slower than 50 ms (a visible hitch) and a steady 60 frames per second.

complaints.text: the top of the page (hero) and scrolling out of it feel laggy
the end of the page (pushing past the end, where the bottom panel grows) feels laggy

changes.text: New work, the user's second priority: look for cheaper ways to draw effects that look the same, and show each one to the user to accept or reject.
Two small items (the endless sweep animations and the image sizes) are parked until the bigger style fixes have phone results, so effort stays on the largest slow frames.

Your two ideas checked: complex CSS is not the cause; the cost is how many elements each change touches. The images use more memory than needed but cost nothing per frame. Seven ranked fixes follow, scene-scope first.
A fix for slow style recalculation is being built (fix-scene-scope): it narrows how the page pauses its hidden scenes. After a Chrome check it goes to the phone next.
Your decision: style recalculation is now the top priority. The phone first records where style time goes in A and B; the robot-finger check and the other tests follow.

Your sitting: on the hero and at the end of the page, the best build felt quite a bit smoother than the original. Your idea that style recalculation causes the lag is now being checked by a new helper.

Cause found for the blinking small profiles: each time the carousel swaps a picture in or out, the whole page re-lays out (P14 on the phone). A fix that keeps the pictures in place is next, right after your sitting.

From your request: a tool change is being designed so that tests and simulator checks can run side by side, while timing tests keep the Mac to themselves. A reviewer now checks the waiting lock-tool changes.

New rule from you: checks that need an iPhone but no timing number now run on the iPhone simulator on the Mac; the real phone stays for timing tests and your sittings. The carousel test (P14) started at 17:42 (about 30-35 min); your sitting comes next.
Coming up for you: a sitting on the phone that compares the original page with today's best build (the countdown fix and F3 together).

The robot finger turned out to play every stroke as a quick flick, so its results so far don't count (tool problem I-042). The countdown fix's robot test (P-032) was void; all robot-finger tests wait for the tool fix. The phone runs the carousel test (P14) meanwhile.
Touch-listener blind test scored: neither you nor the second tester felt a difference (2 of 4 pairs each, the same as guessing).
Phone tests approved and queued: the avatar carousel at the top (P14) and the softer blur easing for the card reveal (P-038).
The iOS Simulator was checked as a stand-in for the phone: not usable as a judge of smoothness. The real iPhone stays the judge.
Your three blind swipe pairs for the countdown fix all came back 'same'. It now lands only if the robot-finger test (P-032) passes.
Layout containment (lc-cq3) dropped: the work moved elsewhere, the slow frames did not get shorter.
F3 removed the 106-118 ms hitch in the middle of the page in 4 of 4 scripted runs; the F1 variant stopped.

items.title: Your idea: style recalculation (about 19-20 ms) causes the lag
items.fixes: You saw style recalculation taking about 19-20 ms at times, more than a 60 Hz frame allows (16.7 ms). Your two guesses: complex nested CSS makes selector matching slow, or the images (rotation, resizing) cost work every frame. You also asked about smaller images and plain-CSS effects.
items.gate: Find out whether either guess explains the slow frames before anything is built.
items.next: Top priority (your decision). de-style-recalc proposed a fix: pause the page's hidden scenes in a narrower way so fewer elements get their style recalculated. fix-scene-scope builds it, checks it in Chrome, then it goes to the phone next.
details: User hypotheses from C-013 notes (lead relay 18:3xZ): (1) selector matching cost from nested/complex CSS; (2) image rotation/resizing per frame, image sizes, cap render triggers at 60 fps via native CSS. Checked (de-style-recalc, style-recalc-images.md 30eaa11): H1 nested CSS REFUTED (no nesting shipped, matching ~3 %; the spikes are invalidation scope with nested Layout in RecalculateStyles); H2 images oversized in memory (~35 MB derived) but not a per-frame cost. Ranked: 1 scene-scope (this item), 2 r4-v3, 3 st5 (hero-carousel), 4 fwreskip, 5-6 anim-transform, 7 image-size.
fix-scene-scope (lead 18:5xZ): variants on B: V1 narrow the :where(*) scene pause, V1b pause by API, V2 flip early, V3 panel + R4; Chrome check, then a W Timeline phone block ahead of P-039.

items.title: Cheaper look-alike effects (user priority 2)
items.fixes: Some effects cost a lot to redraw. A cheaper way to draw something that looks the same is fine with the user. Agents look for such swaps and show each one to the user as a proposal.
items.gate: The user accepts or rejects each proposal on the console page. Only an accepted one becomes a fix with a phone test.
items.next: Two research agents count the costs on the computer first, then send the first proposals.
details: User priority 2 (lead 19:1xZ), right after style recalc. de-illusion-style: style/layout costs; de-illusion-composite: compositing, layers, blur; ts-proposals: console Proposals page (read, visual compare, Accept/Reject/Request change). Counts first, at most 2 batched Chrome holds each before first proposals, queued after scene-scope and the de-counts pair; no phone before the user accepts; accepted -> fix topic + phone ticket via mgmt-ops.
